utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we begin today, there's a matter that I'd like to deal with in private session. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless there's any other matter to be raised, we'll bring in the next witness. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just something very quickly to note for the record. Yesterday there was mention during testimony of Mr. Trifkovic of a taped statement that was taken during his consultation with the Defence. We asked the Defence for a copy of that under 67(A)(ii). The Defence told us, in fact I think they proactively approached us, I should note, to tell us that in fact the interview had not been taped and no such tape exists, and of course we accept that representation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Garaplija. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, before you start giving evidence, I'd like to draw your attention to a specific rule here at the Tribunal. Under this rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt or could provide evidence that you have committed a criminal offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If I can say just one more thing for the record and that is that this witness is here pursuant to a subpoena and therefore has not volunteered to testify on behalf of Dr. Karadzic. I think that's important to be said for the public and for the witness also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't see the point of raising this in court. It's evident. Yes. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Garaplija.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for waiting for the interpretation, and I would ask you to continue like this so that the interpretation could be carried out in time. Could you please tell me your first name, last name, and your father's name?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Edin Garaplija, son of Ibro, and mother Ajsa [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I was born in Pljevlja, on the 14th of November, 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was your profession before the war?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Before the war I was construction contractor. I was in the construction business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you change your job during the war and when?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: At the start of the war, I was a reserve member of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And from June, I was a member of the State Security Service of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was part of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From June. Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: This was 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was your post? What was your job in that service?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Well, you could say that I carried out a lot of operative jobs, starting from the administration for operative work, then through the technical sector, the administration for analysis, and then most recently I was appointed as deputy chief of the centre for the secret surveillance of the State Security Service. I was also the leader of an anti-terrorist team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hold that position also in June 1996, and if not, what was your position in June 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: As I said, I was head of team for combat against terrorism and also deputy chief of the service for secret surveillance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As part of your job on that anti-terrorist team, did you interview Nedzad Herenda in June 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. As part of the operative action code-named Eagle, the head of the service, director of what was already AID, the service for information and documents, which was the successor of the State Security Service, Mr. Kemal Ademovic, gave our team the assignment to investigate the activities linked to the organising of the para-unit called Seve, headed by Nedzad -- sorry, including Nedzad Herenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the members of Seve. What kind of organisation is it? When was it established and by whom?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: As I said, Nedzad Herenda was a member of the Seve unit which -- as the war operations began in April 1992 and he established -- Alija Delimustafic, then head of the MUP, established this unit Seve and incorporated it into the MUP. I would like to stress here that neither then nor later, as we discovered in our 1996 investigation, within the systemic organisation of the State Security Service was there any need, nor was it envisaged, to establish any military unit like Seve. The existence and the work of that unit within the State Security Service was completely secret, and only a few senior leaders knew about it. In addition to Alija Delimustafic, the minister, the head of the State Security Service -- or, rather, one of the leaders and later the head of the SDB, Nedzad Ugljen, knew about them and managed their work. After the existence of the Seve group was revealed to the public in mid-1996, Nedzad Ugljen was killed in Sarajevo shortly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's request: Could the witness be asked to speak more naturally. It is very difficult to interpret this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to clear up a few things. You said it was incorporated into the MUP, and you say it was a military unit of the state security. Could you tell the Chamber what is the connection?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I just was noting the interpreter's request to the witness. I wonder if that could be passed on, that the witness be asked to speak more naturally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm just slightly puzzled as to what that entails. Mr. Witness, the interpreters have asked you to speak more naturally. I think I know what they mean. Perhaps if you could enunciate your words a little more clearly, perhaps that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. The witness is cutting his sentences into bits and pieces that are difficult to connect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. These are very difficult matters, but I'm trying to be as precise as I can because I have great appreciation for your time and the time of the Defence team. If something is not clear, I can try to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let's continue, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, it would be better for you to make pauses between sentences, not between words. Could you tell me what was the connection between the MUP and the state security whose armed organ were Laste. To avoid any confusion, I'm talking about the MUP and the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Karadzic is mistaken. We are discussing the unit called Seve, not Laste.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Let me clarify. Within the structure of the Ministry of the Interior, in addition to the public security sector, otherwise known as the uniformed police, there existed the State Security Service, also known as the secret police. As I said before in one of my previous answers, Mr. Herenda as a member of the Seve and the Seve unit itself were appointed as a paramilitary unit of the State Security Service, circumventing the whole structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the position of late Ugljen in that organisation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I have already answered this question. I said Ugljen was one of the leaders from the time the Seve were established until his death, and for a while he also held the highest position in the State Security Service as its undersecretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what this operation code-named Eagle involved?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Under the code-name Eagle, an operative action was conducted to detect and expose the unit Seve and especially its leader Mr. Herenda and subsequently documenting its activities and documenting its chain of command and operative activities. We received our orders for this action from the head of the service, or, rather, the Agency for Investigation and Documentation, Mr. Kemal Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the assassination of Nedzad Ugljen ever investigated successfully, and did it have anything to do with the operation Eagle?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: After exposing the whole group, documenting the crimes they committed and especially those by their member Nedzad Herenda, a trial was rigged. A show trial was organised in which the internal structures of the Bosnian forces of law enforcement and justice tried to hide under the carpet the existence of the Seve unit. As far as I'm concerned and my colleagues who were involved in the process, we were made to be part of this show trial. This was in June -- correction, July 1996. A couple of months after we were arrested -- and I emphasise here that I was detained together with my colleagues in complete isolation, without any contact with the outside world save for the appointed counsel, counsel appointed to me by the service wherein I had no way to get any information. So after a couple of months, Nedzad Ugljen was killed in one of the suburbs of Sarajevo as one of their inconvenient witnesses who was a direct leader and controller and knew a lot about the people who gave orders to the Seve group. Later, as the process unfolded, as the trial continued while we were imprisoned, a judgement was pronounced where we were convicted for kidnapping and killing Nedzad Herenda. And this was a deliberately false judgement because everybody knew we were police officers who acted on orders. And only after two years of serving the sentences we were given, I addressed the International Court for Human Rights which had a branch office in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was called Human Rights Hall, presided by a French Judge, Michele Picard. Our judgement was rendered null and void by that human rights court and a judge rapporteur, Giovanni Grasso. This court ordered a retrial, following which we were released from prison and pardoned in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So before July 1996 -- or, rather, did you interview Herenda in your official position in June 1996 or before?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As I said before, there was this operative action properly recorded by the service within the framework of the law. We were members of the agency for investigation and documentation, and we conducted an interview with Nedzad Herenda for 72 hours, as the law allowed us, on the official premises of the agency. The interview was conducted within the framework of our powers and authority, and it was recorded on audio and video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Herenda provide you in the course of the interview with enough information about the personnel and the tasks of the Seve group, with all the information you needed, in other words?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I have to stress that Nedzad Herenda was extremely well trained and attempted to conceal his activities, but we, the investigators, used the ruse and presented the initial information we had as information we received from his partner and accomplice in their criminal enterprise, a man named Dragan Sosic, who also used another name, Dragan Bozic. As a result, Herenda made confessions that shocked us about his own activities and those of other members of the Seve unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what was so shocking about what you heard in that interview?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: All the terrorist activities pursued by the Seve unit, beginning with sniping assassinations, setting explosives and such, were conducted completely outside of the system and very compromising to Bosnian defence. The only one who could profit from such activities was the opposing side, at that time the Army of Republika Srpska. We were shocked by the sniping assassinations and the brutality displayed by Herenda and his co-perpetrators in these crimes, because until then, we knew of such things perpetrated by the other side alone, by their constant sniping and artillery attacks through the city. We had never expected anyone from, conditionally speaking, our side to be involved in such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Herenda, in that interview, say anything about the murder of a French soldier in Sarajevo during the war? But before that, Mr. Garaplija, what you discussed, did the Seve unit do those things only in Sarajevo or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I can recall after 17 years has elapsed between that interview and today, and thanks to the proofing done by the Defence team who reminded me of my interview to the OTP back in 1998 while I was doing time after the rigged trial that I mentioned a couple of minutes ago, the Seve unit mostly were active within Sarajevo, but some of their activities were conducted outside the city and even abroad. But because of the very short time that we had with Herenda as investigators, we had to focus on the most important things that we had assessed as being crucial or key for our investigation, and one of them being the murder of a French UNPROFOR member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What -- could you tell us what Herenda said about that, where the murder happened and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date exactly. I think it was 1995. Herenda explained that he had been given a mission to open sniper fire at Serb positions. This is what he would often do from the building known as the Executive Council's building in downtown Sarajevo, from which spot, in accordance with his testimony, he fired at that French UNPROFOR member. I don't know whether he had any orders to do so or whether he did it on his own, but certainly what he did was deeply compromising for our struggle, for our defence, and for our officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the Executive Council's building or the government's building. Could you please explain where it is located and what are the most important facilities around it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That building is in the very centre of the town at the location of Marin Dvor, close to the land museum, across the street from the Holiday Inn Hotel. That building was renovated after the war, and now it's called the building of Greek-Bosnian Friendship, and it houses institutions of the Council of Ministers of Bosnia-Herzegovina currently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the circumstances under that French soldier was murdered?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I cannot recall all the details, but after the Defence team showed me a tape of my testimony, I recall that the French soldier was putting up fortifications along one of the streets which was exposed to the Serbian side so that the Serbs could fire at passers-by and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, at the time of that murder, was there any investigation taking place? Who was suspected of being the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any investigations nor who conducted those at the time because I was not involved in documenting those events at the time. I did so several years later. What I do know, though, is that certain Bosnian officials stated that the Serb side was responsible for the death of that French soldier. Whether those officials knew who the real perpetrator was, this is something that I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me, did Herenda do that as part of a particular action or operation? Do you know whether he received any remuneration or award of a non-monetary kind?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's just a minor point. The -- so far the questions have been appropriately phrased as, "Did Herenda tell you X," and now the question is phrased more in -- you know, did Herenda do that. The foundation that's been laid is what Herenda has told this witness in the past, and I think the questions should be framed in that manner in terms of what this witness learned from Herenda. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I concede. Let me rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Herenda say anything to you about any reward or remuneration?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Herenda said that for that action and for other actions as well, he did receive certain amounts to the tune of thousands of German marks, which were used as money in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this was a small fortune for people living in besieged Sarajevo. I can't recall how much money he received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at 1D7607. It is a short video recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "NM: So the last time we were talking about killing of a soldier from the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] EG: Well, Herenda said he was shooting, that he was ordered to do so by Ugljen so as the United Nations would blame the Serbs. He received a payment for that in the range of 2.000 marks."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this refresh your memory, Mr. Garaplija?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Since this is my statement I gave in -- to the OTP 12 years ago, I think, in 2000, I think that what I said then is more precise than what I say today. As Mr. Karadzic said, it really did jog my memory since that took time -- took place several years after I'd been arrested and after Herenda had been murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please admit this video as an exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to identify that portion by time or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is an excerpt, Mr. President, so that's the only thing on that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, very well. Yes. We'll receive it as the next -- the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2906, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me retrieve another document to refresh your memory. You said that you did not remember the date of this incident concerning the French soldier. You said it was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up 1D7056 to the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you understand English, Mr. Garaplija?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this jog your memory? Was this in April, mid-April, and does this document refer to that incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I would have to read the text first before I can answer, if you allow me some time to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe paragraph 5 would be of assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could turn the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, are you happy with the English? You have no difficulty reading the English document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no difficulty, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is mention of a forklift tractor. It is said here that the first bullet hit the forklift tractor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. This could be the aforementioned incident since it concerns a French soldier, but what I don't see here is the location of the incident. This is probably on page 1 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I do believe that this is mentioned here. A moment, please. The second line of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. In the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Erecting anti-sniper barriers near the Holiday Inn; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. That's the -- the location that Herenda said that he engaged in sniping a French soldier was close to Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn the page so that we can see the rest of paragraph 5 and paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see (c) and (d) which discusses the distances for Bosnia-Herzegovina Army and distances between positions of the Bosnian Serbs and that location?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it says here that the BSA would have had three possible firing positions at approximately 300 metres, and under (d), that the BH Army would have one position at 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I please -- I move to tender this document, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2907, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned another incident which was chosen to be investigated because of the shortness of time, and that was an explosion killing the wife of General Halilovic. Did Herenda tell you anything about that explosion which killed the wife of General Halilovic and her brother, and if he did so, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Herenda did admit that he was a co-perpetrator within the Seve unit who planted that explosive device with a view of eliminating General Halilovic. It is important to know that General Halilovic was at the time Supreme Commander of the Bosnian Army, and a couple of months before this attempted assassination which killed his wife and her brother, he'd been removed from that position because he'd publicly opposed division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That could have been the motive, because in his statement, Herenda said that they'd done it on purpose knowing who the target was, that the target was one of the highest ranking officers of the BH Army, but that they'd been convinced that he was a traitor, enemy of the state, and that he was portrayed to them in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did he describe to you the way the action was carried out?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Herenda explained that they placed the explosive beneath the balcony or terrace of General Halilovic, that they monitored his movements electronically, that they had tapped his phones, were doing surveillance on him and other measures, and that at the appropriate time were prepared to liquidate him, to activate the explosive device. It was just by pure luck that General Halilovic saved himself because he was late in arriving home, and in the meantime, unfortunately for his wife and her brother, her brother was wearing a camouflage uniform, clothing, and he resembled General Halilovic, and at that moment when he appeared on the balcony, on the terrace, Herenda and his associates activated the explosive device, as a consequence of which General Halilovic's wife and her brother were killed while General Halilovic at that point in time was not in that apartment, and he survived the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Garaplija. And thanks to the fact that the General, as an expert, survived, was he able to find out who did this? Was it possible to guide the investigation in any particular direction? In other words, did General Halilovic have any idea of who was responsible for the attack?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Halilovic was absolutely convinced that this was an assassination attempt, conceived, planned, organised, and he survived this assassination attempt. However, none of these acts by the Seve unit was criminally prosecuted, brought to trial, because a large team of people worked to conceal these crimes. And as proof of that is the staged trial of myself and my colleague, because we discovered the existence of the Seve unit. And then later, there were investigations carried out about the activities of the Seve unit and their organisation, so that General Halilovic actually did not manage, even though he did request that -- that this be clarified, he did not manage to get the authorities to bring the case to trial and to bring evidence to light about the act in a regular legal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how was this presented to General Halilovic, and what was the public told? What was the official position on this matter?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: The public was told that this was a shell launched by the Serbian Army, or the Army of Republika Srpska, that it was a guided projectile of the Maljutka type, as far as I can recall from Herenda's statement, because he and the other perpetrators left a Maljutka wire, which is a characteristic of that particular projectile. They left that behind in order to create the impression that this was a Maljutka launched from Serb positions. General Halilovic himself doubted this version of events, and from what I learned later from reading the newspapers and from his public statements, he sought additional investigations which established that the explosion was not the result of a shell or a guided projectile, but that it was possible that the explosion was the result of a planted explosive device.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Garaplija. And did Herenda tell you that just the wires were found at the place of the explosion or did they leave other traces in their attempt to present this as a result of an incoming projectile?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I remember the wire and Herenda's testimony about the wire, but I cannot now say with any degree of certainty whether there was any other evidence. But again, I can say that that act deeply compromised the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because that act of liquidation was carried out against one of the top-ranking commanders of the Bosnian Army, which later most probably shook the morale among most of the Bosnian units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Garaplija. I would like to again refresh your memory. Of course it's been a long time since then, but I would like to 1D7608 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "EG: So as I said before, Halilovic was running late, while his wife and her brother stepped out on the terrace. The brother of Halilovic's wife was in a military camouflage uniform, so Herenda and other accomplices of this terroristic act thought that it was Halilovic, because they were observing them from -- from about -- from a hundred metres of distance. And at this moment, they activated the explosive device, which -- which resulted in the death of Halilovic's wife and her brother. "The -- the previous plan and the previous organisation of the Herenda -- Herenda's group was to use the investigation commotion, so they hoped that the assassination would be successful and that much fuss would be made out of that. So they -- they decided to -- to plant a piece of a wire which usually remains after the activation of a remote-controlled missile. That type of missile was often used in Bosnia, known under the name Maljutka. Herenda explained later that was supposed to turn the investigation into the wrong direction, and the official report would be -- the official report would be that the Serbs from the mountain hit Halilovic's apartment with a missile."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And does this now jog your memory, Mr. Garaplija?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, and I think I said it before, and I mentioned similar information before about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the Maljutka shell, does it leave any fragments at the site of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I'm not a ballistics expert or a military officer in order to be able to answer this question, and I don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this excerpt under this number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2908, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we discuss what happened to you after this official operation, are you able to tell us if you gave up investigating other Seve cases, and did you just investigate these two cases on a priority basis, or did you also investigate other cases involving the Seve?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic's question is not clear to me. As far as I know, from 1996 when I was detained in the put-up trial proceedings against me, I was no longer in the service, and I did not work after that in the police investigation organ, so I really cannot say whether the acts and the documents that we had acquired during our investigation from Mr. Nedzad Herenda, I don't know if they were ever brought to trial or if the Prosecution procedure was ever completed, because since that time I have been -- I was no longer in the police structures, and I was in private business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. Am I correct when I said that you said that a lot of things shocked you, but these two cases you emphasised as a priority because of lack of time; is that correct? Because you did not have sufficient time at your disposal for investigations. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 13 of the transcript, the witness said that he was shocked by a lot of things, but these two particular cases all the more so, because they only had 72 hours to document the cases.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We investigated the other crimes by the Seve such as the liquidation of captured soldiers and civilians in the great big park in the centre of town, something that was committed personally by Nedzad Herenda. We had scores of witnesses about this. We also investigated other sniper actions by the Seve units throughout the Grbavica neighbourhood. We investigated the activities of the Seve in the execution and bringing in of confidential documents and funds inside and out of Sarajevo. There were a number of acts that we investigated. However, these two, because of their brutality, were particularly shocking because one person involved was a member of the United Nations, the peacekeeping forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina entrusted with maintaining the peace and security of all the parties. And in the second case, this was a high-ranking army commander and leader of the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us whether this model of proclaiming somebody as an enemy of the state was something that was used in other cases, and did Herenda inform you about that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I don't know about other cases, but I can tell you about my own experience. When my colleagues and I documented crimes perpetrated by the Seve, Bosnian leaders treated me as the enemy of the state. That's why this show trial was organised. That's why I was placed in solitary confinement for over a year in very difficult conditions. Just to illustrate, I will tell you that this was the only cell in the Sarajevo prison without heating and without a window, and I was kept there from June until May next year. That means one whole winter. I was also subjected to various methods of pressure. They wanted to break me. And later, after the conviction which found me an abductor in that show trial and after I was imprisoned, there were several attempts to kill me. And again I must stress the role of the human rights court which used the method of out-voting, where the Presiding Judge Michele Picard had two votes, and only thanks to them was my judgement quashed and a retrial ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me about this incident in Veliki Park with captured soldiers and civilians who were killed? Who were those soldiers and civilians? Line 16, page 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: First of all, this information is irrelevant; and secondly, the notification we were provided with basically consisted of a Defence draft statement and the notification in the subpoena application stated that the two incidents that have just been discussed were the only incidents that would be dealt with through this witness. So I object to going into this further incident on those two bases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But this witness is a viva voce witness, and then he himself mentioned that incident, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: He did, Your Honour, but first of all, the mere fact that a witness is a viva voce evidence doesn't absolve the Defence from the requirement to provide adequate notice to the Prosecution. That notice was provided in the form of the subpoena application. In fact, the Defence's latest Rule 65 ter filing refers specifically to that subpoena application as the 65 ter notice. That subpoena application only mentions the two incidents that have just been discussed in testimony. This other incident is contained in the OTP information, but it's contained in the OTP interview. It's irrelevant, and the Prosecution wasn't notified about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the basis on which you are saying it's irrelevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It deals with the execution of a number of Serb civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, would you like to respond to this objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can also withdraw the question, although it does follow from the witness's evidence. Let me move to the last question then before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the last one before the break. Perhaps my last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I shall not ask you about the names of the prominent members of the Seve group, but I was curious about one name in particular. Did you mention a physician, a pathologist, and what was his role in the Seve unit?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: In his interview, Herenda mentioned a pathologist, Ilijas Dobraca, who is no longer alive, but his job was to provide medical certificates after certain assassinations, to cover them up in other words, listing a different cause of death, natural causes or something else, which would side-track the investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Herenda. I have no further questions -- oh, sorry. Sorry. Thank you, Mr. Garaplija. I have no further questions. I have every sympathy for you and all that you have been through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have break for half an hour and resume at 5 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before the Prosecution starts its cross-examination, Mr. Garaplija, you told us that while you were imprisoned, a judgement was pronounced where you were convicted for kidnapping and killing Nedzad Herenda. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I'm not sure if you told us about the killing of Herenda. How was he killed, or how did he die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Herenda was not killed. It is the indictment that said "attempted murder." So at that time at least he was still alive, at the time when we were on trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you don't know where about Herenda now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know where Herenda is nowadays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Garaplija.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I just have a few questions for you this morning. I'd like to start with just one question about the incident of the shooting of the French soldier that you described. You said that Herenda told you that he had fired from the Executive Council building. And just to be absolutely clear, I'd like you to clarify that the Executive Council building was in ABiH-held territory at the time.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. The building of the Executive Council was under the control of the BH Army throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said one of the areas of your investigations into the Seve activities in the course of your interview with Mr. Herenda was the sniping actions throughout the Grbavica neighbourhood. And again, I'd just like to clarify that those sniping actions were actions where the Seve unit were sniping from ABiH-held territory into Serb positions in Grbavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. That is what Nedzad Herenda told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And all this -- all these things that Nedzad Herenda told you that you recounted to the Court today, those were all things that he told you during the course of your interview with him in June 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Correct. Within the space of three days, that is to say, the 72 hours that we had the right under the law to interrogate Herenda in the Agency for Investigations and Documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right. Because he was under arrest at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And before his arrest, you had never spoken to Herenda; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: One month before his arrest, we initiated the Eagle operation, whose purpose was to carry out surveillance on and document the activities of Nedzad Herenda and other members of the Seve unit. Within those 30 days, we kept Herenda under surveillance. We documented his activities, that he had a service vehicle, a service weapon, et cetera, although officially speaking, that unit did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Garaplija. My question was simply to have you confirm that before his arrest you had never spoken to Herenda. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: No. No, I did not. I never talked to him before the arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you referred in your direct examination to your arrest and conviction following this interview with Herenda. Just to be precise, you were arrested specifically for the mistreatment of Herenda in the course of the interview, in particular abduction, maltreatment in discharge of duty, and attempted murder; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. That was a bogus indictment that was quashed later before the Human Rights Hall, and the domestic judicial institutions were ordered to conduct a retrial where a verdict, a conviction, was handed down for overstepping official authority and the unlawful imprisonment that we endured, one year, one month, and one day. After that, I personally instituted another proceedings before the Human Rights Hall that resulted in the quashing of the entire judgement, and I have since never been tried for anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Mr. Garaplija, what you've just described is untrue. You were initially convicted, as you say. Your case did go before the Bosnian Human Rights Chamber in 2000. They did find a violation of your rights. There were then further proceedings at the Bosnian Supreme Court in 2000 where they quashed the conviction for abduction, maintained the conviction for mistreatment in discharge of duty and attempted murder, and then you brought a further application to the Bosnian Human Rights Chamber and, in 2002, that chamber found that there had been no violation of your rights in the 2000 Bosnian Supreme Court judgement that had convicted you for mistreatment and discharge of duty and attempted murder. That's actually what happened, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said, except I didn't mention that in the second proceedings I was found guilty of overstepping my official authorities, not attempted murder. So the abduction and attempted murder did not feature in the appeals proceedings. And shortly afterward, I was released from the state prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in your earlier answer you had said that in the second proceedings before the Human Rights Chamber, that those proceedings resulted in the quashing of the entire judgement. That's entirely false. That Human Rights Chamber decision upheld your conviction; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That is correct. Perhaps I told it wrong, but I said I was never again tried in this case. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Could we have 65 ter 24563, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The document that you're about to see, Mr. Garaplija, on your screen is this second proceeding before the Bosnian Human Rights Chamber, and this is dated the 12th of April, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 of this judgement, decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And here the chamber sets out the lengthy prior proceedings including its -- at paragraph 14 it describes its own earlier decision where it had found a violation of your rights in your first trial. It then goes on to describe the further proceedings in the Bosnian state courts, and at paragraph 18 describes the Bosnian Supreme Court proceedings of October -- decision of October 24, 2000. And it explains, in the second sentence, that the Supreme Court found it established that the applicant, and that's you, "hit the injured party with his fist, bound him to the pipe of a radiator, inserted a wooden club between his hands when he was already cuffed and hit him on different parts of his body." And then it goes on to explain how the Supreme Court overturned the conviction for abduction and maintained the conviction for maltreatment in discharge of duty and attempted murder and reduced your sentence. Now, this is what the Supreme Court of Bosnia in the final judgement against you found that you had done to Mr. Herenda in the course of the June 1996 interview; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: The Human Rights Chamber did not deal with the details of the conviction. Instead, as the highest judicial body ordered a retrial, and in this case the Supreme Court did not want me to be present and testify in appellate proceedings, and thanks to a legal advisor from the ICTY, Carl Kenning, who was present in the courtroom when that was said, he informed the Tribunal in The Hague which, as far as I know, issued a note to the Bosnian judiciary and then the Supreme Court held another session where I was allowed to give evidence. In that testimony, I put into the record the written orders for Operation Eagle, which identified us as officers of the Agency for Investigations and Documentation assigned to carry out the arrest of Nedzad Herenda. I maintain with full responsibility that there was no mistreatment of Nedzad Herenda. Instead, one of the operative workers who were in the room with him --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, I'm sorry to interrupt you but you're not answering my question. And my question was simply to have you confirm that this description of what the Supreme Court of Bosnia found in its final judgement against you was indeed an accurate description of its findings, not whether you agree whether the findings were correct or not, but whether that indeed reflects what the Supreme Court found.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I was just trying to explain the role of the Human Rights Chamber, and what is written here corroborates what I've been saying. The Chamber did not go into the details in its second proceedings. Instead, it found that the original error committed by the Supreme Court by failing to invite me to the session when deciding about the validity of the judgement constituted a violation of my human rights, and this is precisely what is said here. The second-instance decision of the Human Rights Court, the Human Rights Chamber, orders the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina to allow me to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, this is the second proceeding before the Bosnian Human Rights Chamber. It's quite clear because they reference their own earlier proceeding in your case. So this is the second proceeding. And if we go to page 12 of this decision, under "Conclusion" at the bottom, the Chamber concluded unanimously that your complaint of a lack of impartiality was manifestly ill-founded and, by 12 votes to 1, that there had been no violation of your rights. So contrary to what you've just stated, the second proceeding in the Bosnian Human Rights Chamber found no violation of your rights in relation to the Supreme Court's final judgement against you in 2000; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That is precisely what I was trying to say, that this is the second proceedings before the Human Rights Chamber, not the Supreme Court. The Human Rights Chamber did not go into the details of the judgement of the Supreme Court except in the part that my right to attend the session and present my defence was violated. And provide new evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Garaplija. I have no further questions. I'd just like to tender this judgement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6103, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Court's leave, I should like to note that along with this judgement of the Human Rights Chamber, there is a dissenting opinion of Judge Giovanni Grasso, which is very important and clarifies a lot of what I have been saying. This dissenting opinion is attached to the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It is admitted into evidence in its entirety. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Garaplija, what about Mr. Herenda tell you about Grbavica? What were they targeting with snipers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it arose from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It did. Your Excellencies, on page 29, line 3, the Prosecution suggested the target of this action, but I would not like to discuss before the witness before we get his answer. But for all the parties it's page 29, line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this -- I mean, this doesn't arise from cross-examination in any proper way. I was -- the witness had already mentioned in his direct examination sniping actions in Grbavica. I was simply clarifying who was on what side of the confrontation line. It does not open the door for Mr. Karadzic to now ask questions about precisely who was being targeted, particularly as this is going to go into irrelevant tu quoque evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You asked the witness, or you stated in putting your question, that the Seve unit was sniping from ABiH-held territory into Serb positions in Grbavica. On my part as well I wanted to put a question with respect to that regard, so I would allow the accused to continue. What was your question, Mr. Karadzic? What were -- who were the targets of sniping? If you could answer the question, Mr. Garaplija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Herenda told us they targeted Serb positions and soldiers and sometimes also civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that all you heard from Herenda about the targeting civilians? Civilians from what -- which side? You mean Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm talking about the side controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska. And we were impressed by one detail in this investigation. When asked how he knew those people were civilians, Herenda said that he selected women wearing black because that identified them in his eyes as Serb women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any further re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, you talked about the Executive Council building. Do you know whether the sniper was on that building throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Herenda related that he fired from that building as well. Whether this was the case in the case of the French soldier, whether he was at that position, which direction he aimed at, I'm not sure. I can't recall. But what I'm sure about is that he did mention the Executive Council building, because this is the only building of that height in Sarajevo and of that character.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the transcript page. At one point in time during your examination-in-chief you told us that you were shocked because you never expected anyone from "our side" to be involved in such things. So separate from the incident that involved a French soldier and Halilovic's wife's death, what else did you have in mind by such things?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: As I said earlier, sniping at civilians, for instance, murder of captured civilians and prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from Herenda that that unit also did sniping against Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Except in the case of the attempted liquidation of one of the then commanders of military police of the BiH Army named Ismet Bajramovic, whom Herenda tried to murder by sniper fire together with his associates, I did not hear from Herenda of any other instances of sniping at civilians. I apologise to Your Honours. I did hear of another case, opening fire at soldiers during the Trebevic operation where Seve unit sniped one unit involved in that operation. On that occasion, as far as I can remember, two guards of a commander were murdered, two sentries within that unit which got out of control during that operation. These are the two cases that I heard about in my interview and investigation of Nedzad Herenda. But since more than 17 years have passed, I do not exclude a possibility that there were other cases. I could have mentioned other cases in my interviews with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, if Your Honours have finished asking questions, I'd seek leave to ask one further question in cross-examination that arises out of Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Further Cross-examination by Ms. Gustafson:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, just in relation to the attempted liquidation of one of the military police commanders, Ismet Bajramovic. Now, in relation to that incident that Herenda told you about, Herenda was tasked to assassinate Ismet Bajramovic, who was not only a commander, but he was also a notorious organised crime boss, and that was because of a dispute between Mr. Bajramovic and Bakir Alispahic, a senior DB official, over unsettled bills and drug trafficking; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct. Ismet Bajramovic had a very long rap sheet. At the beginning of the war, he got involved in Alija Delimustafic's cabinet or office. He was, as I said, within the Ministry of the Interior. And throughout his stay in Sarajevo, until the day when Herenda sniped at him, he had performed military police tasks as one of the commanders. After he was wounded by sniper fired by Herenda, Bajramovic was dislocated to a European country, I think Germany, for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Garaplija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, would you like to ask re-examination -- have a re-examination on this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellencies. Let us clarify concerning the answer to your question. Further Re-examination by Mr. Karadzic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Part of which structure was that unit whose two sentries were murdered by Seve during the Trebevic operation or the Trebevic action?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: The commander of that unit was Musan Topalovic, who soon afterwards was arrested and liquidated the same day in front of one of the command headquarters of BH Army within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's clarify this point. Was Celo a member of the Seve unit or was he a target? Or are there two Celo? I mean Celo Bajramovic.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Ismet Bajramovic, aka Celo, was a target of the Seve unit. He wasn't a member of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the other Celo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Please be precise. Who is this other Celo?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ramiz Delalic, also known as Celo.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Ramiz Delalic, aka Celo, was never their member nor was he a target of the Seve. Pursuant to Herenda's testimony, I do not have any knowledge of him being a part of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Garaplija. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to the The Hague to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a short break?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That would be helpful just to log out and log in and rearrange our materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.41 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect to Your Honours, before I -- I'm asked anything, I would like to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, General. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before doing so, if the counsel for General Krstic could introduce himself for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. My name is Tomislav Visnjic. I represent General Krstic in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Yes, Mr. Krstic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You took a decision on the basis of Mr. Karadzic's request. However much his request is legally founded, for me it is senseless, inhumane, and constitutes an act of violence against me. The finding and the results of an examination by a psychiatrist and his colleagues concerning my health and the reasons for my return to the Detention Unit mean nothing to him. He simply has his goal. He wants to attain it at all cost. This is his matter. But I cannot suffer such inconsiderate trampling over me for his attainment of that goal. My health is severely affected. In such conditions, with all the ramifications of my PTSD and all my problems with concentration, and for all these reasons the very idea that I'm supposed to speak before this Chamber, that circumstance causes a great deal of stress to me. I warned Mr. Karadzic of this, but of course, this means nothing to him. Driven by the goal that he wants to attain, he imagined that I don't want to be his Defence witness. He thinks that I was talked into that, and this is not true. What I've suffered throughout the seven years that I've been in British prisons, not just that one attack, all that has affected me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Krstic. I should ask Mr. Visnjic if we can continue in public session or we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I offered all the available options to General Krstic, options on how he's supposed to say what he wants to say, particularly the information about his health. If he wants so, I will move for that to take place in open session [as interpreted], but it is up to him to give his final decision. He knows the options and it will be up to him to say what he wants to say and determine the method of saying that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Krstic, I take it you understood my point. Are you happy to continue in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that I've suffered throughout the seven years that I was in English prisons, it is known to some members of the Chamber and to the public, and by the same token, it should be known to Mr. Karadzic as well. All this has left a deep scar in my mental health. I am physically very poor. My sight is poor and damaged. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: further torture, humiliation. What I need is peace of mind, but unfortunately, I must say that my peace of mind has been perpetually disturbed by Mr. Karadzic through his repeated requests. My recovery over the past year has not been adequate by a long shot by the conditions prevailing in the Detention Unit. Although I'm under constant monitoring and therapy of a team of psychiatrists who care for my health, my disease has not been checked, and this is cause for my grave concern. Bearing in mind everything that I've said and what my lawyer and counsel has submitted to the Chamber, with all due respect to the decision handed down by this Chamber this morning, I still maintain my position that, for health reasons, I am not able to testify in these proceedings. Not just in these proceedings. I hope that you are not going to ask me to discuss details of my health with you, something that I discuss with my physicians, given my state. It will be irresponsible [Realtime transcript read in error "responsible"] on my part to concede and to agree to take the solemn declaration concerning the aforementioned. Thank you very much for your indulgence and for listening me out -- hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: General Krstic, is it your position that your mental and physical health is in such a state of disturbance that you do not think that you could give testimony in this case which would adequately reflect the questions that you might be asked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. Exactly. No physician can explain how I feel. Except for me, I know what my state is, and I know the nightmare that I'm going through today because of the consequences that lie at the root of what I was telling you a moment ago, because of the causes that brought about those consequences.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may address the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber knows that I did take into account fully what General Krstic experienced recently, and that is why I just wanted to put a few questions to him. So I'm kindly asking to be permitted to ask him those questions, but I will completely accept the Trial Chamber's decision about the further course of this testimony, but I do want to put a number of questions, the least possible number of questions, and that they be entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not to speak in front of the witness, but I reiterate the position I said this morning in closed session about my position on my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is minded to take a lunch break now for an hour, and we'll consider the issue. So we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krstic, the Chamber has carefully considered your statement and we understand your concerns. Nevertheless, we maintain the decision issued this morning that your testimony should proceed today as planned. Let me assure you, however, that your health will not be discussed during your testimony, and the Chamber also instructs the Prosecution and the Defence not to go into the incident in the UK as it is not relevant to these proceedings. The Chamber will, as always, keep the case under review. If at any time we think it is in the interest of justice to take a short break, we will do so. Likewise, you are at liberty to ask for such a break during the course of your testimony. Now, Mr. Krstic, could you please take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect in regard of your decision, I really stand by my position that I stated. I simply cannot work to the detriment of my health. I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go further, I'd like to hear from the parties. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any observations to make?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I called the witness taking a lot of care and taking into account everything that he experienced, but I'm accused or charged with the events that occurred in that zone. I have no substitute for this witness. No one else can provide the answers to important questions, and in view of this situation, I seek to put at least two questions. The questions are between myself and the witness, and the answers are between the witness and the Trial Chamber. I would at least like to put these questions to him. But I fully understand the position of the General and everything that he has been through, and I think that you saw that in -- this morning in my conduct and in my words that I took that fully into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours. The only position I would have is to respond to what Mr. Karadzic just said is not entirely accurate. For one, the -- I don't know, of course, what questions he intends to put, but the guidance we've been given from the Defence is that the questions they would put are exactly what was put in the grounds for the subpoena as a relevant motion of what they would ask the witness about. That information is available in the 92 quater testimony of Mr. Lazic, exactly what they would try to seek on one basis, and I advised my friend during the break that if they withdrew their objection to the Lazic 92 quater motion, that is one way they could get that. The second point is -- this was not raised by Mr. Krstic's lawyers, but the record does not -- the record of Mr. Krstic's prior testimony does not indicate that the -- he would give the answers that Mr. Karadzic is requesting. So I don't take a position on what steps the Chamber should take next, but I just want to correct that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: General, you have to be aware that a refusal to give testimony when you've been called to the court calls into question the issue of a potential contempt of court and the consequences which may flow from that. As you are represented today in court by Mr. Tomislav Visnjic of counsel, the Court would like you, Mr. Visnjic, to explain to the General in clear terms what the position is and what the consequences may be under the statute of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I talked with the General during the pause, and he's completely acquainted with the possible consequences according to the Tribunal procedures. We did not know what your decision would be, but I did acquaint him of the consequences pursuant to Rule 77 in his particular case. I would like to say one more thing. I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to two errors in the transcript. One is on page 41, line 9, where it was stated that it was my recommendation to the General to speak about his state of health in open session, but actually it should have been that I recommended he speak about it in closed session, but he accepted this other option. This is one thing. The other second thing, on page 43, which I think is more important, line 25, in the translation into the Serbian, the General was told that during his testimony "your health will not be discussed." This is what Judge Kwon said, but actually the translation he got was that his trial will not be discussed. So perhaps this could bring about some confusion and it could have had an effect on his final decision. So actually the translation that he -- or the interpretation he received should be corrected to be in line with what Judge Kwon said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: General, having heard what your attorney Mr. Visnjic has said, do you still maintain your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the most important thing to me is my health, and I stand by my position without any intention to enter into any kind of confrontation with anyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will rise for 15 minutes. --- Break taken at 1.14 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry to interrupt. I think there's a possible error in the transcript I just wanted to bring to your attention. It's at page 42, line 14. It reads, where Mr. Krstic was speaking: "It will be responsible on my part to concede and to agree to take the solemn declaration," and I was alerted to that by Mr. Tieger that the word might have been "irresponsible."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That may be. Do you confirm that, Mr. Krstic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krstic, before proceeding further, the Chamber would like to have before it additional medical information in relation to your statement that testifying in this trial would be detrimental to your health. Therefore, the Chamber orders the Registry to ensure that another more detailed medical report is produced evaluating Mr. Krstic's physical and mental health. In particular, this report should focus on addressing the question of whether testifying in this trial would indeed be detrimental to Mr. Krstic's health, and if so, in what way. It should also consider the issue of whether he's mentally fit to testify at all. In that respect, the medical examiner should consider whether Mr. Krstic has a basic capacity to understand the questions put to him and give rational and truthful answers to those questions. The said report should be provided to the Chamber and the parties in this case by the 8th of March, 2013. Following the receipt of the report of the -- report, the Chamber will decide its next course of action. Mr. Krstic, you may be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there are no other witnesses for today, but I take it we can continue on Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a problem. I didn't know who you were addressing that to, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless there's anything to be raised, the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of February, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.00 p.m.,
